identification.summary: Suckfly is the Symantec name for a China-based cyber-espionage group. Symantec's May 2016 reporting attributes a series of attacks beginning in April 2014 to it [S3][S5]. Symantec believes the group developed the custom Backdoor.Nidiran specifically for espionage and delivered it via strategic web compromise [S1]. The group first came to public attention in March 2016 through its use of stolen code-signing certificates [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Attacks attributed to Suckfly by Symantec begin April 2014 [S3][S5]; certificate-signed tools in use from early 2014 [S1][S2]. Symantec found the activity in late 2015 [S2].
identification.notes: Suckfly is Symantec's name. The imported record lists APT22 (Mandiant), BRONZE OLIVE (Secureworks) and Group 46 as aliases, and MITRE tracks the group as G0039; I could not open those vendor pages and no cited source here states the mappings, so they are not added or independently confirmed. A MISP galaxy commit discovered in search results shows Suckfly was at one point confused with APT41 and later corrected; do not merge facts across those clusters. Microsoft has no record of a Typhoon/Sleet name for this group in the imported record (msName empty).

attribution.confidence: Symantec states the group is China-based and traced activity to three IP addresses in Chengdu, China [S1]. No source gathered attributes Suckfly to a named PRC government organization.
attribution.basis: Symantec infrastructure observation: activity originated from three separate IP addresses, all in Chengdu, China [S1]. This is a vendor assessment, not government attribution.

objectives: Espionage is the stated purpose of the Nidiran backdoor per Symantec [S1]; the end objective is not established in the sources gathered.

sectors: Healthcare (Indian business unit of a US provider)
regions: South Korea (Seoul companies whose code-signing certificates were stolen) [S1][S2]
targeting.notes: Symantec's May 2016 report lists one of India's largest financial organizations, a large e-commerce company and its shipping vendor, one of India's top five IT firms, two government organizations and the Indian business unit of a US healthcare provider [S3][S4]. Victim names are not public. A secondary blog claims defense and energy targeting and six government victims; that conflicts with the Symantec-based coverage and is not used.

capabilities.summary: Symantec reports the group stole code-signing certificates from nine companies in central Seoul and used them to sign hacking tools and malware [S1][S2]. The exact theft method is unknown; Symantec's most likely scenario is malware inside the victim companies that searched for and extracted certificates [S2]. Tools included a Windows brute-force SMB scanner signed with a certificate belonging to a South Korean mobile software developer, which led to discovery in late 2015 [S2][S6]. The custom Backdoor.Nidiran was delivered via strategic web compromise [S1]. The stolen certificates were still valid when found [S2].

diamond.adversary: China-based group tracked by Symantec as Suckfly; operators' identity and sponsor not established [S1].
diamond.capability: Stolen Seoul code-signing certificates, custom Backdoor.Nidiran, signed brute-force SMB scanner, strategic web compromise delivery [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Three IP addresses in Chengdu, China as origin of activity [S1]; compromised victim organizations in Seoul as certificate source [S1][S2].
diamond.victim: Indian finance, e-commerce and logistics, IT, government and healthcare organizations; South Korean certificate holders as enabling victims [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints and SMB networks; trust in valid code-signing certificates by security tools [S2].

gaps: Could not open the primary Symantec blogs (March and May 2016), MITRE G0039, Secureworks BRONZE OLIVE or Mandiant APT22 pages (network fetch failed); findings rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
Alias mappings APT22 (Mandiant), BRONZE OLIVE (Secureworks) and Group 46 from the imported record are unverified here; Mandiant APT22 documentation was not found.
No government attribution or named sponsor; Chengdu IPs are a vendor observation only.
No activity after 2016 was found in the sources gathered; current status of the group is unknown.
Certificate theft method, victim names and the group's end objective are unknown.
Imported references (Slideshare, IBM X-Force collection) were not reviewed.
Removed unverified claims: DiMaggio statement on no benefit from government intrusions, and the central-government network-software victim role (not confirmed in searches).

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Certificate stores and code-signing infrastructure at contractors and software vendors, are key terrain [S2]. STEP 2: Signed tools can pass trust checks, so defenders relying on signature validity are disadvantaged [S2]. STEP 3: Template is certificate theft, signed scanner and backdoor, strategic web compromise [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued regional espionage via targeting of Indian organizations; MDCOA is use of stolen certificates from allied or coalition vendors to sign tools against US and partner networks (inference, not sourced). Candidate indicators: validly signed binaries from unexpected publishers, SMB brute-force scanning, and traffic to Chengdu-based IPs [S1][S2]. Evidence is from 2014 to 2016 and may be dated.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track certificate-revocation notices from industry vendors and treat signed-binary alerts as potentially hostile [S2]. (2) Authorities: certificate revocation and supplier notification involve commercial and foreign entities; coordinate through established DIB and partner-nation channels. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize IT suppliers and code-signing infrastructure [S2][S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partners in India and South Korea only through approved intelligence-sharing channels.
